solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Cryptic clue concept introduces name of mathematician (9)

indicatorNotes.Cryptic: something cryptic is hidden or scrambled, so the letters of CLUE IDEA are jumbled
indicatorNotes.introduces: the concept brings in N, adding it to the fodder

blocks.note: used as it stands
a concept is an idea
n = name, a standard abbreviation

annotation.surface: A remark about how a cryptic clue's central idea brings in a mathematician's name.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is self-referential: it seems to describe crossword-setting itself. 'Cryptic' looks like a description of the clue but is the instruction to scramble.
annotation.definitionFit: Euclid was the Greek geometer, and the adjective formed from his name means belonging to him.

entries.clue: The things over there promoting English attitudes (5)

indicatorNotes.promoting: in a down clue, promoting E moves it up to the top of the word

blocks.note: E = English, lifted to the front
THOSE = the things over there, with its E taken out to be promoted

annotation.surface: Someone is pushing English attitudes, perhaps in a far-off place.
annotation.walkthrough: The E already at the end of THOSE simply climbs to the start of the entry.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a group's characteristic spirit and outlook are its attitudes.

entries.clue: Jokes about broken nose in public to conceal wrongdoing (5,4,6)

indicatorNotes.about: the jokes go around everything else
indicatorNotes.broken: a broken nose is knocked out of shape, so its letters are rearranged
indicatorNotes.in: the rearranged letters sit inside the word for public

blocks.note: cracks = wisecracks, jokes; they go outside
overt = open, public
NOSE rearranged, placed inside the word for public

annotation.surface: Someone cracks jokes about a broken nose in public, perhaps to hide what really happened.
annotation.walkthrough: A double sandwich: one container sits inside another. The jokes open after their first letter to take in the rest.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: removing the traces of where one has been is hiding what one did wrong.

entries.clue: Tavern recently denied opening without prior instruction (8)

indicatorNotes.denied opening: the word is refused its first letter

blocks.note: an inn is a tavern
LATELY = recently, minus its opening L

annotation.surface: A pub that was recently refused permission to open.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Opening' reads as a pub's opening, but here it is the first letter of LATELY.
annotation.definitionFit: What you do by nature, from birth, needs no teaching beforehand.

entries.clue: Cross endless circles from the outside (8)

annotation.definitionNote: adjectival phrase, as in 'pressure from the outside' = external pressure

indicatorNotes.circles: to circle something is to surround it

blocks.note: eternal = without end; it goes around
a cross is an X, as on a ballot paper

annotation.surface: An instruction to cross out endlessly repeating circles from the outside edge.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like a verb or an adjective but is the letter X; 'endless' is not an end-deletion but a whole word meaning without end.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something that comes from the outside, like outside pressure, is external.

entries.clue: Be aware of only steam and water? (6)

blocks.note: steam and water are two of water's three states: gas and liquid, but not the solid one

annotation.surface: A puzzled question about what it means to notice nothing but steam and water.
annotation.walkthrough: Split the answer as NOT ICE: leaving out the frozen state is what 'only steam and water' describes. The question mark flags this playful second definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the first sense, to register or be aware of; the second is a split-word pun.

entries.clue: Force wingless insect to zoom in (5)

indicatorNotes.wingless: the wings of a word are its outer letters, so they are removed

blocks.note: F = force, as in physics
LOCUST without its first and last letters

annotation.surface: Making an insect whose wings are gone move in close.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Wingless' fits a locust literally, but the wings removed are the letters L and T at each end.
annotation.definitionFit: A camera sense: zooming in and sharpening on a subject both mean concentrating the view.

entries.clue: Planting tree covers nothing up (6)

indicatorNotes.covers: the tree wraps around the other word
indicatorNotes.up: in a down clue, a word read upwards is reversed

blocks.note: a fig is a tree; it goes outside
NIX = nothing, reversed and placed inside the tree

annotation.surface: A newly planted tree hides nothing as it grows up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Planting' looks like gardening to match the tree, but the sense needed is setting something firmly in place.
annotation.definitionFit: Planting a post or a flag means setting it firmly in position.

entries.clue: Emissions from second vehicle seemingly still supporting walking (6,9)

indicatorNotes.seemingly: flags that 'second vehicle' is read loosely as a B-grade car, CAR B
indicatorNotes.supporting: in a down clue, a word supporting another sits beneath it

blocks.note: a car is a vehicle
B is second, as in B-list; together 'car B'
on foot = walking
a still is a photograph, a print; it goes under the walking phrase

annotation.surface: Pollution from a second car, and even walking seems to leave a mark.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Still' is not an adverb but a photographic still. 'Seemingly' excuses reading 'second vehicle' as a B-car.
annotation.definitionFit: The term names the total greenhouse gas a person or activity emits, so it stands for emissions.

entries.clue: Old container getting hit resulted in trouble on motorway (5,4)

indicatorNotes.in trouble: letters in trouble are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: anagram fodder
M = motorway, as in the M1; it comes last, beneath the anagram

annotation.surface: An old barrel is struck, causing chaos on the motorway.
annotation.walkthrough: The Caribbean instrument was first made from discarded oil drums, so an old container that gets hit describes it exactly.
annotation.definitionFit: A description: the percussion instrument is a recycled oil barrel that is played by striking it.

entries.clue: Deprived person of shelter and books (4-3)

blocks.note: a haven is a shelter
OT = Old Testament, a set of books

annotation.surface: Someone deprived of a roof over their head and of reading matter.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Deprived of' reads as one phrase, but 'of' is only the link.
annotation.definitionFit: The haves and the have-nots: the term names the poor, those lacking what others possess.

entries.clue: Test run blocking payment avoiding tariffs (3-4)

indicatorNotes.blocking: the letter sits in the middle of the payment, blocking it

blocks.note: to tax is to test or strain
a fee is a payment; it goes around R
R = run, as on a cricket scoresheet

annotation.surface: A trial run that holds up a payment to escape import duties.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Test run' looks like one phrase but splits in two, and 'test' is the verb sense of straining someone.
annotation.definitionFit: Tariffs are taxes on goods, so goods that escape them are free of tax.

entries.clue: Show off clothing on specialist channel (5)

indicatorNotes.clothing: the clothing of a word is its outside, its first and last letters

blocks.note: outer letters of SpecialisT
a rut is a channel or groove

annotation.surface: Someone flaunting their outfit on a niche television channel.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Show off clothing' reads as flaunting an outfit and 'specialist channel' as niche TV; both pairs split.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to walk with a proud swagger is to show off.

entries.clue: Boy going over small hill defending Republican’s rebellious music (4,1,4)

indicatorNotes.going over: to go over is to turn back, so the letters are reversed
indicatorNotes.defending: the hill surrounds the Republican, protecting it

blocks.note: 'Boy!' and 'Cor!' are both exclamations of surprise; COR reversed
a knoll is a small hill; it goes around R
R = Republican

annotation.surface: A young man walks over a hillock guarding a Republican's defiant music.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Boy' looks like a lad but is the exclamation 'Boy!', which in British speech is COR.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the 1950s genre was the defiant youth music of its day.

entries.clue: Fictional royal family leads regal broadcast (4,4)

indicatorNotes.leads: to lead is to go at the head, so the family word is placed in front of the rest

blocks.note: kin = family
REGAL rearranged

annotation.surface: A royal family in fiction heading a stately television programme.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Royal family' reads as one phrase; split it, since 'royal' belongs to the definition and 'family' to the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Shakespeare's invented monarch is a royal who exists only in fiction.

entries.clue: What officials should do in middle of tower? (4,5)

blocks.note: a keep is a castle's central tower, and the middle of anything is its core

annotation.surface: A question about what referees should do in the centre of a castle.
annotation.walkthrough: The second definition is playful, flagged by the question mark: split the answer as KEEP'S CORE.
annotation.definitionFit: Officials at a game record the points; the second sense is a split-word pun on a castle keep.

entries.clue: Back section of Niagara Falls at a distance (4)

indicatorNotes.section of: only a part of the phrase is taken

blocks.note: niagaRA FAlls, read right to left

annotation.surface: A view of the rear part of Niagara Falls from far away.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Back section' reads as the rear of the falls, but 'back' tells you to read the letters in reverse.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, somewhat literary: far off, at a distance.

entries.clue: Renegade gambler enjoys streak for second time (8)

indicatorNotes.enjoys: to enjoy something is to have it, so the gambler takes the streak in
indicatorNotes.for second: the streak goes in place of the second of the two letters named

blocks.note: a better is someone who bets
a ray is a streak of light
T = time; the second T of the gambler is swapped out

annotation.surface: A gambler has a winning streak for the second time.
annotation.walkthrough: 'For second time' reads as 'again', but it means: in place of the second T.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a renegade deserts a cause, and so is a traitor.

entries.clue: Trap hidden by sadist is not fair? (8)

annotation.definitionNote: the definition is a description (one who is not fair), the answer a noun

indicatorNotes.hidden by: the trap is concealed inside the sadist

blocks.note: a brute is a cruel person; it goes around the trap
a net is a trap

annotation.surface: A trap set by a sadist: surely that isn't fair?
annotation.walkthrough: 'Not fair' sounds like a protest at cruelty, but fair here means blonde, so the definition describes a dark-haired person.
annotation.definitionFit: Fair means light-haired, so a woman with dark hair is one who is not fair.

entries.clue: Language refresher regularly used (4)

indicatorNotes.regularly used: only letters at regular intervals are used

blocks.note: the even letters of rEfReShEr

annotation.surface: A language refresher course that gets regular use.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Language refresher' reads as a course, but 'Language' alone is the definition. Erse is a crossword favourite.
annotation.definitionFit: An old name for Scottish or Irish Gaelic, a Celtic language.

entries.clue: Item repeatedly left in hotel room, ie foolishly getting left inside (8)

indicatorNotes.foolishly: letters behaving foolishly are all over the place, so they are jumbled
indicatorNotes.getting: the jumbled letters get, or receive, the extra letter into their middle

blocks.note: H = hotel in the NATO alphabet
anagram fodder
anagram fodder
L = left, placed inside the jumbled letters

annotation.surface: A guest keeps foolishly forgetting things in their hotel room.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Repeatedly left' sounds like absent-mindedness, but the item is left in wills, generation after generation.
annotation.definitionFit: A family treasure is bequeathed down the line, so it is left again and again.

entries.clue: Buddhist monument misplacing heart on large religious figure (2,4)

indicatorNotes.misplacing heart: the middle letter is moved to another spot, here the end
indicatorNotes.on: in a down clue, one piece sits on top of the next

blocks.note: STUPA with its middle U moved to the end
L = large, as on clothing labels

annotation.surface: A Buddhist shrine has lost its centre, sitting on a huge statue of a holy man.
annotation.walkthrough: A stupa is a dome-shaped Buddhist shrine. 'Misplacing' does not delete the heart, it moves it.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the apostle is one of Christianity's central figures.

entries.clue: Lack of light entertainment commercial breaks (6)

indicatorNotes.breaks: the commercial breaks into the show, splitting it

blocks.note: a show is entertainment; it goes around the commercial
an ad is a commercial

annotation.surface: Light entertainment on television interrupted by commercial breaks.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Light entertainment' and 'commercial breaks' are both TV phrases; each has to be split, with 'light' going to the definition and 'breaks' being the instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Where an object blocks the light, the dark patch left behind is an absence of light.

entries.clue: Something carried by paramedics initially stops this person convulsing (9)

indicatorNotes.initially: take the initial letters of the words

blocks.note: first letters of Stops This
someone retching, heaving convulsively

annotation.surface: Paramedics stop someone having a fit.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Initially' looks as if it applies to 'paramedics' before it, but it takes the first letters of the two words after.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the portable bed for patients is one of the things ambulance crews carry.

entries.clue: State of many temples in northeast China (5)

blocks.note: NE = northeast
in Cockney rhyming slang, china (plate) = mate, a pal

annotation.surface: A country full of temples, somewhere in the northeast of China.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface places the country in China geographically, but China is the rhyming slang word for mate.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the Himalayan country is dotted with Hindu and Buddhist temples.

entries.clue: Unit consisting of fifty united soldiers (5)

blocks.note: L = 50 in Roman numerals
U = united, as in football club names
soldiers = men

annotation.surface: A military unit made up of fifty soldiers working as one.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Unit' looks like a military unit, but it is a unit of measurement.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this is the SI measure of luminous flux, one unit among many.

entries.clue: Fuji’s area for growth? (7)

blocks.note: not the Japanese mountain but a variety of apple
not a business's growth area but a place where fruit trees grow

annotation.surface: A question about where Mount Fuji's area might expand.
annotation.walkthrough: Fuji suggests the Japanese mountain, but a Fuji is also a popular apple, and apples grow on trees in a particular kind of plot.
annotation.definitionFit: Apple trees such as the Fuji are grown in a planted plot of fruit trees.

entries.clue: Metal pump with no pressure — try it out first (7)

indicatorNotes.out: letters put out are knocked out of order
indicatorNotes.first: the anagram comes first, ahead of the pump remnant

blocks.note: TRY IT rearranged
PUMP without either P (pressure)

annotation.surface: A pump has lost pressure, so test it before anything else.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Try it out' reads as test it, but 'out' is the scramble signal. The metal is named after Ytterby in Sweden.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: it is a rare silvery metallic element.

entries.clue: Case of anchovies secured by fish stand (5)

indicatorNotes.Case of: the case of a word is its outer shell, its first and last letters
indicatorNotes.secured by: the fish holds those letters inside it

blocks.note: an eel is a fish; it goes around the anchovy letters
outer letters of AnchovieS

annotation.surface: A tin of anchovies held in place by a fish on a stall.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Case of anchovies' looks like a crate of fish, but is the outside of the word.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by type: the artist's frame for holding a canvas is a kind of stand.

entries.clue: Flesh finally tore threadbare trousers with lots of holes (4-5)

indicatorNotes.finally: 'finally' points to the word's final letter, the last it offers
indicatorNotes.trousers: used as a verb: to trouser is to pocket, so the word goes around the others

blocks.note: worn = threadbare; it goes around the rest
meat = flesh
last letter of torE

annotation.surface: Someone's flesh finally tore through a pair of threadbare trousers full of holes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Trousers' is a verb here: to trouser is British slang for pocketing, so the threadbare word swallows the others.
annotation.definitionFit: Wood or cloth that grubs have bored through is riddled with holes.
